summary: Describes the motivation and benefits of using Segment Routing in large data centers that run BGP, and a design for deploying it with both MPLS and IPv6 data planes. It is informational guidance, not a new protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: Huge buildings full of computers need good traffic directions. This explains why giving each packet its own route list helps there, and how to set it up.

questions: what is segment routing in data centers
why use segment routing instead of ecmp
subtitle: Using Segment Routing to improve traffic flow in large data centers.

tldr.problem: Large data centers use Equal-Cost Multipath (ECMP) routing, which makes traffic paths unpredictable and hard to engineer. Faults are difficult to isolate, and there is no good way for hosts to control which path their traffic takes.
tldr.mechanism: Segment Routing (SR) lets packets carry an explicit list of hops, computed at the source and carried in the packet itself. BGP distributes Prefix Segments (segment IDs for each router), and hosts or controllers can build label stacks to steer traffic along chosen paths.
tldr.outcome: Data center operators get deterministic routing, better troubleshooting, per-flow traffic engineering without per-flow state at intermediate routers, and simplified operations without needing new signaling protocols like LDP or RSVP-TE.

facts.value: MPLS and IPv6 Segment Routing Header

today: RFC 8670 is Informational guidance for deploying Segment Routing in large data centers. Major data center operators have adopted these techniques to improve traffic engineering and reduce operational complexity. The RFC does not define a new protocol but describes how to combine existing RFCs (8402 for SR architecture, 8669 for BGP Prefix-SID, 8277 for BGP Labeled Unicast) in a practical data center design.

sections.title: Large Data Centers and Segment Routing
sections.content:
Segment Routing (SR) applies source routing to modern networks: instead of computing paths at each hop, a packet carries an ordered list of instructions called segments. Each segment can be a next-hop, a subnet, a service, or any instruction defined by the network. This RFC applies SR to the BGP-based design used in large data centers, where multiple parallel paths connect every pair of servers.

The RFC uses the BGP Prefix-SID, defined in RFC 8669, to announce that each router can be the target of a segment. When a controller or host wants to send traffic via a specific path, it constructs a segment list and pushes it onto the packet as MPLS labels (or IPv6 Segment Routing Header fields). Each router pops the top segment and forwards based on it; when the last segment is reached, normal forwarding resumes.

This approach requires no new signaling protocols (like LDP or RSVP-TE). It works with the existing BGP and MPLS or IPv6 infrastructure, making it deployable in existing data centers.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of each router deciding where to send a packet, the sender writes the path in the packet. The routers just follow the instructions. No need for a separate route-planning system.

sections.title: Data Center Topology and BGP Prefix Segments
sections.content:
The RFC builds on RFC 7938, which describes a standard Clos topology for large data centers. In a Clos fabric, servers are attached to top-of-rack (ToR) switches, which connect to leaf switches, which connect to spine switches. This creates multiple parallel paths between any two servers.

In traditional BGP routing, each router independently chooses one best path or load-balances across equal-cost paths using ECMP. With Segment Routing, the BGP Prefix-SID extension allows each router to advertise that it is reachable via a segment with a specific index. All routers in the fabric can be configured with the same Segment Routing Global Block (SRGB)—for example, [16000, 23999]—meaning router X is always reached via label 16000 + X across the entire fabric.

This global label allocation greatly simplifies operations. A controller can instruct a host to send traffic via a specific spine by building a label stack: the top label is the spine's Prefix Segment, the next label is the destination ToR's Prefix Segment. Every router understands this globally consistent mapping without configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: Every building (router) gets a number. If everyone agrees that building 5 is always reachable via label 16005, then to send a packet through building 5 on the way to building 11, you just put those two numbers in order in the packet.

sections.title: MPLS and IPv6 Data Planes
sections.content:
The RFC describes two ways to carry segments: MPLS labels and IPv6 Segment Routing Header (SRH).

In the MPLS version, routers use BGP Labeled Unicast (RFC 8277) to distribute both IP reachability and MPLS labels. Each Prefix-SID becomes an MPLS label. When a host sends traffic to a destination via specific spines, it pushes a label stack: the first label steers toward the spine, the second toward the destination. Intermediate routers perform standard MPLS forwarding: they match the top label, forward based on it, and pop it when appropriate.

In the IPv6 version, the Segment Routing Header (SRH) replaces label stacks. A packet with an SRH carries a list of IPv6 addresses representing segment endpoints. Each router processes the active segment (the current IPv6 address in the SRH list), forwards toward it, and advances to the next segment when the active segment is reached.

Both approaches avoid traditional signaling. No LDP session or RSVP tunnel setup is needed. BGP alone carries the topology, and routers derive their forwarding tables directly from the Prefix-SID announcements.
sections.plainLanguage: With MPLS, you write the path as a stack of numbers (labels). With IPv6, you write it as a list of addresses in the packet header. Either way, routers just follow the list and check them off.

sections.title: Operational and Performance Benefits
sections.content:
Segment Routing in data centers enables several improvements over traditional BGP + ECMP routing:

Deterministic paths: With explicit segments, every packet bound for a destination via a specific path takes that path, enabling troubleshooting and load profiling. Unlike ECMP, which hash-randomizes paths, SR gives predictable routing.

Egress Peer Engineering (EPE): A controller can direct outbound traffic to specific external peers. A host sends traffic to a border router via an Egress Peer Segment, telling the border which BGP peer to use for that destination. This avoids per-flow state on the border router itself.

FIB table optimization: Routers can switch all traffic to MPLS-based forwarding at upper tiers, avoiding large IP lookups and reducing table size.

Incremental deployment: SR can be deployed one router at a time. Routers that do not yet support Prefix-SID allocate dynamic labels but still forward traffic correctly because outgoing labels are derived from received labels, not from the Prefix-SID index.

No new protocols: LDP and RSVP-TE, which require complex state management and distributed signaling, are not used. Operators manage only BGP, simplifying the fabric considerably.
sections.plainLanguage: You know exactly where each packet goes. Hosts can pick their exit door without asking intermediate routers for permission. Big routers can drop IP and use simple label forwarding. You can add SR support one router at a time. No complex route negotiation needed.

sections.title: Unified SRGB and Simplified Management
sections.content:
The RFC strongly recommends that all routers in a fabric use the same SRGB (Segment Routing Global Block). This is crucial for operational simplicity. With a unified SRGB, the label for a destination is identical on every router. Troubleshooting is straightforward: label 16011 always means "toward router 11" everywhere in the fabric. Controllers can apply the same forwarding policy to all hosts without per-router translation.

Without a unified SRGB, each router has its own label space, forcing controllers to translate policies for each router and maintain complex mappings. This increases operational burden, reduces clarity, and increases the chance of misconfiguration.

The design also supports the concept of anycast segments. Multiple routers can share the same segment ID for availability and load balancing. For example, border routers might all advertise segment 20, so traffic to segment 20 load-balances across all of them using ECMP, while traffic via a specific border still uses a flow-engineered path with multiple segments.
sections.plainLanguage: If every building has the same number everywhere, life is simple. Label 16005 means spine 5 no matter which router you ask. If different buildings had different numbers at different places, you would need a translation table for every decision, and you would make mistakes.
